title: JSX
subtitle: JavaScript XML — expressions, attributes, fragments, and the rules of JSX
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Writing UIs with React.createElement('div', null, React.createElement('h1', null, 'Hello')) is verbose and hard to read.
whyItExists.solution: JSX is syntactic sugar that lets you write HTML-like syntax inside JavaScript. Babel (or the TypeScript compiler) transforms JSX to React.createElement calls. JSX is not HTML — it has stricter rules and allows embedding any JavaScript expression.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Every React component. JSX is the standard way to write React UI. The .jsx (or .tsx for TypeScript) file extension signals that a file contains JSX.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Environments without a build step. In that case, use React.createElement directly. But in 99% of React projects you have Babel or TypeScript, so you always use JSX.

Spread attributes: . Key rule: adjacent JSX elements need a wrapper or Fragment — this is because JSX compiles to a function call which can only return one value. JSX children: text, expressions, other components, and arrays are all valid children. Null, undefined, false, and true render nothing — useful for conditional rendering. explainModes.technical: JSX compilation target: with the new JSX transform (React 17+, react/jsx-runtime), imports are automatic — no need to import React in every file. Older projects needed import React from 'react' in every JSX file. The pragma: @jsx tells Babel what function to use (default: React.createElement). Custom pragma: @jsx h for Preact. JSX is not HTML — it maps to JavaScript, so properties that conflict with JS reserved words are renamed: class→className, for→htmlFor. Event attributes take functions, not strings: onClick={handler} not onclick='handler()'.
explainModes.deepDive: JSX has a one-root rule because function calls return one value — React.createElement calls can only return one element. Fragment solves this by wrapping in React.Fragment which renders nothing to the DOM. Key-based rendering: JSX arrays must have keys to allow stable reconciliation. The key doesn't need to be globally unique — just unique among siblings. Don't use array index as key when the list can be reordered (it confuses the reconciler). Computed expressions in JSX: {items.map(item => <Item key={item.id} {...item} />)} — map returns an array of elements, which React renders as siblings.

content.text: JSX pitfalls: use `className` not `class`, `htmlFor` not `for`, and `style={{color:'red'}}` (object) not `style="color:red"` (string). All tags must be closed — `<input />` not `<input>`.

questions.question: Why does JSX use `className` instead of `class`?
options: React invented className — it doesn't exist in HTML
class is a reserved keyword in JavaScript, so JSX uses className to avoid conflicts
className is faster than class at runtime
You can use either class or className in JSX — they both work
questions.explanation: JSX compiles to JavaScript, and class is a reserved keyword in JavaScript (used for defining classes). Using class as an attribute name in JSX would conflict with the JavaScript parser. So React uses className (which maps to the DOM element's className property). Similarly, for → htmlFor (for is a JS loop keyword).

faq.q: Can I write if/else inside JSX?
faq.a: Not directly — JSX only accepts expressions, not statements. Instead use: ternary (condition ? A : B), short-circuit (&& for 'render if true'), or move the logic above the return statement. You can also extract complex conditionals into a helper function that returns JSX.
